summary.text: For \(n\ge4913\), set \(K=\pi(n)\) and take all primes up to \(n\) together with \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\); a maximal-divisor argument shows that every \(m\le n\) factors into two members of this set whenever \(n^2\le K^3\), so \(a(n)\le2\pi(n)\). The condition \(n^2\le\pi(n)^3\) is derived from \(2^n\le(n+1)n^{\pi(n)}\), obtained via the middle binomial coefficient, plus elementary exponential estimates on consecutive cube intervals, while \(n<4913\) is covered by \(a(n)\le n\) and \(\pi(n)\ge1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_n=\{1,2,\dots,n\},
\]
and for a finite set \(S\) of positive integers let
\[
S\cdot S=\{xy:x,y\in S\}.
\]
For \(n\ge 1\), define \(a(n)\) to be the minimum cardinality of a subset \(S\subseteq T_n\) such that \(T_n\subseteq S\cdot S\). (The value at \(n=0\) is irrelevant to the assertion and may be set to zero.) Such a set always exists: one can take \(S=T_n\), because \(m=m\cdot1\) for every \(m\in T_n\). In particular,
\[
a(n)\le n. \tag{1}
\]
Write \(\pi(n)\) for the number of primes at most \(n\).

We will prove the stronger estimate
\[
a(n)\le 2\pi(n)\qquad(n\ge 4913), \tag{2}
\]
and then deal with the finitely bounded range \(2\le n<4913\) using (1).

## 1. A covering construction

We first establish the main factorization lemma behind the construction.

### Factorization lemma

Suppose that \(1\le K\le n\) and
\[
n^2\le K^3. \tag{3}
\]
Then every integer \(m\) with \(1\le m\le n\) can be written as \(m=xy\), where each of \(x,y\) is either a prime at most \(n\), or an integer at most \(K\).

Indeed, fix such an \(m\). There are two immediate cases.

* If \(m\) is prime, write \(m=m\cdot1\). Here \(m\) is a prime at most \(n\), while \(1\le K\).
* If \(m\le K\), again write \(m=m\cdot1\), and both factors are at most \(K\).

It remains to consider a composite \(m>K\). Since \(m\le n\), condition (3) gives
\[
m^2\le n^2\le K^3. \tag{4}
\]
There are now two cases according to the sizes of the prime divisors of \(m\).

First suppose that \(m\) has a prime divisor \(p\) satisfying
\[
p>\left\lfloor\frac mK\right\rfloor.
\]
Write \(m=pq\). We claim that \(q\le K\). To see this, write
\(m=K\lfloor m/K\rfloor+r\), where \(0\le r<K\). Since \(p\) is an integer strictly larger than \(\lfloor m/K\rfloor\),
\[
pK\ge K\left(\left\lfloor\frac mK\right\rfloor+1\right)>m.
\]
If \(q>K\), then \(q\ge K+1\), and hence \(m=pq>pK>m\), an impossibility. Thus \(q\le K\). Also \(q\ge1\), and \(p\le m\le n\). Consequently \(m=pq\) is a factorization of the required kind.

It remains to treat the case in which every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) obeys
\[
p\le \left\lfloor\frac mK\right\rfloor. \tag{5}
\]
Among all divisors of \(m\) that are at most \(K\), choose a largest one, say \(d\). This collection is nonempty because it contains \(1\). We claim that
\[
\frac md\le K.
\]
Suppose otherwise. Then \(m/d>K\), so in particular \(m/d>1\). Therefore \(m/d\) has a prime divisor \(q\). Since \(q\mid m/d\), it is also a prime divisor of \(m\), and (5) gives
\[
q\le \left\lfloor\frac mK\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]
Moreover, \(m/d>K\) implies \(dK<m\), and hence
\[
d\le \left\lfloor\frac mK\right\rfloor. \tag{7}
\]
Multiplying (6) and (7), or equivalently multiplying the inequalities \(dK\le m\) and \(qK\le m\), gives
\[
dq\,K^2\le m^2.
\]
Using (4), we obtain
\[
dq\,K^2\le K^3,
\]
and because \(K>0\), this implies \(dq\le K\). On the other hand, because \(q\mid m/d\), the integer \(dq\) divides \(m\). Also \(q\) is prime, so \(q>1\), and hence \(dq>d\). Thus \(dq\) is a divisor of \(m\), no greater than \(K\), and larger than the chosen maximal divisor \(d\), a contradiction. This proves \(m/d\le K\). Therefore
\[
m=d\cdot \frac md
\]
is a factorization in which both factors are between \(1\) and \(K\). The factorization lemma is proved.

Now define
\[
S_{n,K}=\{p\le n:p\text{ is prime}\}\cup\{1,2,\dots,K\}.
\]
Because \(K\le n\), this is a subset of \(T_n\). The factorization lemma says that every \(m\in T_n\) belongs to \(S_{n,K}\cdot S_{n,K}\). Thus \(S_{n,K}\) is an admissible covering set. Its cardinality is at most the sum of the cardinalities of its two displayed parts, so
\[
|S_{n,K}|\le \pi(n)+K.
\]
By the definition of \(a(n)\), we have proved
\[
\boxed{\ a(n)\le \pi(n)+K\quad\text{whenever }1\le K\le n
\text{ and }n^2\le K^3.\ } \tag{8}
\]

## 2. An elementary lower bound for the prime-counting function

We next prove the explicit estimate
\[
n^2\le \pi(n)^3\qquad(n\ge4913=17^3). \tag{9}
\]
The starting point is the inequality
\[
2^n\le(n+1)n^{\pi(n)}. \tag{10}
\]
We give all details.

Let \(0\le k\le n\), and consider \(\binom nk\). For every prime \(p\), let \(v_p\bigl(\binom nk\bigr)\) be the exponent of \(p\) in its prime factorization. We need the elementary bound
\[
p^{v_p(\binom nk)}\le n \qquad(n>0). \tag{11}
\]
To justify it, recall that counting the multiples of \(p,p^2,p^3,\ldots\) among the factors of a factorial gives
\[
v_p(N!)=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^j}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently,
\[
v_p\left(\binom nk\right)
 =\sum_{j\ge1}
 \left(
 \left\lfloor\frac n{p^j}\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac k{p^j}\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac{n-k}{p^j}\right\rfloor
 \right). \tag{12}
\]
For any positive integer \(q\), because \(n=k+(n-k)\), the corresponding difference of floors in (12) is either \(0\) or \(1\). Furthermore, it is zero when \(p^j>n\). If \(L\) is the largest integer such that \(p^L\le n\), there are at most \(L\) potentially nonzero summands. Hence
\[
v_p\left(\binom nk\right)\le L,
\]
which gives (11).

Every prime occurring in \(\binom nk\) is at most \(n\), and unique prime factorization together with (11) therefore yields
\[
\binom nk
 =\prod_{\substack{p\le n\\p\text{ prime}}}
 p^{v_p(\binom nk)}
 \le \prod_{\substack{p\le n\\p\text{ prime}}}n
 =n^{\pi(n)}. \tag{13}
\]

The binomial coefficients in row \(n\) are all bounded by the middle coefficient \(\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\). This follows, for example, from
\[
\frac{\binom n{r+1}}{\binom nr}=\frac{n-r}{r+1},
\]
which shows that the coefficients increase up to the middle, together with the symmetry \(\binom nr=\binom n{n-r}\). Since the sum of all \(n+1\) coefficients is \(2^n\),
\[
2^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk
 \le(n+1)\binom n{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.
\]
Applying (13) to the middle coefficient proves (10).

We now compare the two sides of (10) more sharply. We need the following elementary exponential estimate: for every integer \(m\ge17\),
\[
(m+1)^{3+3(m+1)^2}<2^{m^3}. \tag{14}
\]
First,
\[
3+3(m+1)^2\le4m^2 \qquad(m\ge17), \tag{15}
\]
because the difference between the right and left sides is
\(m^2-6m-6\), which is positive for \(m\ge17\).

Second,
\[
(m+1)^4<2^m \qquad(m\ge17). \tag{16}
\]
At \(m=17\), this is the direct calculation
\[
18^4=104976<131072=2^{17}.
\]
For the induction step, for every \(m\ge17\),
\[
(m+2)^4\le2(m+1)^4.
\]
Indeed,
\[
2(m+1)^4-(m+2)^4=m^4-12m^2-24m-14>0
\]
for \(m\ge17\). Thus, if \((m+1)^4<2^m\), then
\[
(m+2)^4\le2(m+1)^4<2^{m+1},
\]
proving (16) by induction.

Combining (15) and (16), and noting that \(m^2>0\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(m+1)^{3+3(m+1)^2}
&\le(m+1)^{4m^2}\\
&=\bigl((m+1)^4\bigr)^{m^2}\\
&<\bigl(2^m\bigr)^{m^2}
 =2^{m^3},
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (14).

We can now prove (9). For every \(n\), choose the unique integer \(m\ge0\) satisfying
\[
m^3\le n<(m+1)^3; \tag{17}
\]
such an \(m\) exists by taking the integer part of the cube root of \(n\). If \(n\ge4913=17^3\), then (17) forces \(m\ge17\).

Set \(x=\pi(n)\), and suppose, contrary to (9), that \(n^2\nleq x^3\). In particular, we may use the weaker inequality
\[
x^3\le n^2.
\]
By (17),
\[
x^3\le n^2<(m+1)^6.
\]
It follows that
\[
x<(m+1)^2, \tag{18}
\]
for otherwise cubing \(x\ge(m+1)^2\) would give \(x^3\ge(m+1)^6\).

From \(n<(m+1)^3\) we have \(n+1\le(m+1)^3\), and by (18),
\[
\begin{aligned}
(n+1)n^x
&\le (m+1)^3\left((m+1)^3\right)^{(m+1)^2}\\
&=(m+1)^{3+3(m+1)^2}\\
&<2^{m^3}\\
&\le2^n.
\end{aligned} \tag{19}
\]
Here the strict inequality is (14), and the last inequality follows from \(m^3\le n\). But (19) contradicts (10), which says \(2^n\le(n+1)n^x\). Therefore the supposition was impossible, and (9) follows.

## 3. Completion of the bounded-ratio proof

Let \(n\ge4913\), and choose
\[
K=\pi(n).
\]
There is at least one prime at most \(n\) (indeed, \(2\le n\)), so \(K\ge1\). Also \(K\le n\), since there cannot be more than \(n\) primes among the \(n\) integers \(1,\dots,n\). Finally, (9) says precisely that
\[
n^2\le K^3.
\]
Thus (8) applies and gives
\[
a(n)\le\pi(n)+K=2\pi(n).
\]
Since \(\pi(n)>0\), division gives
\[
\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le2\qquad(n\ge4913). \tag{20}
\]

For the remaining range \(2\le n<4913\), (1) gives \(a(n)\le n<4913\), while \(\pi(n)\ge1\) because \(2\) is prime and \(2\le n\). Hence
\[
\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le4913. \tag{21}
\]
Combining (20) and (21), and observing that \(2\le4913\), we conclude that for every integer \(n\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{\frac{a(n)}{\pi(n)}\le4913.}
\]
Thus the ratio \(a(n)/\pi(n)\) is bounded as \(n\to\infty\), as claimed.
